summary: Followed up the open gap about how the diverged peer was reconciled. Registered a successor harness (assurance_generated_test.go) that replays the same five-node legal history and adds a per-node timeline: leadership, state, term, last index, applied index and log-store bounds for every node immediately after the heal and at 200/400/700/1000/1300 ms, plus the peer's FSM Restore count and applied-command count — enough to distinguish a snapshot install from an AppendEntries repair without touching production logic or reading RPCs off the wire. Local construction feedback already distinguishes the previous receipt's two indistinguishable candidates: at the first sample the successor was still leader at term 3 with store 0/0, three nodes sat at store 1..4 with applied index 4, and the previously partitioned leader sat at store 5..7 with last index 7, applied index 4 and term 3 — i.e. that node had installed the successor's snapshot (lastSnapshotIndex 4) yet kept its stale suffix and its advertised last entry at index 7. The peer's own reconciliation to store 1..4 with zero restores is therefore not a snapshot install and not attributable to the successor's empty log store, so the sender and sequence remain unidentified and are carried as a refined necessary gap rather than guessed. The interpretation stays unresolved (source-only this batch) while recording the counterevidence — a compaction/snapshot-only explanation of the peer's repair is refuted, and installing a snapshot does not reset a follower's advertised last entry when lastLogIndex stays above lastSnapshotIndex — together with the standing narrowing that the leader-side loop is asserted only within its executed single-peer basis (witness CheckRun 7772ad1b5b154d498a27a79806bb0ea7), and the retained five-node receipt CheckRun b9b56ddf3d7d43319db460b87846f71f which refuted generalisation of that loop. Structural validation returned valid=true.
